content_voiceover: This slide gets into the molecular mechanism that underlies TTP, and it's a favorite for board questions on ADAMTS13 biology. On the left, under flowing blood, VWF strings anchored to the vessel wall recruit platelets through the platelet receptor GPIb, and ADAMTS13, the metalloprotease, sits right at that site to regulate VWF length. On the right is the domain map of VWF, with the A1 domain binding GPIb and collagen, the A2 domain containing the actual ADAMTS13 cleavage site at tyrosine 1605 to methionine 1606, and the A3 domain also binding collagen. The critical concept is that ADAMTS13 can only access and cleave that Tyr1605-Met bond in the A2 domain when VWF is unfolded by shear force, shown here by the arrows labeled Force pulling the A2 domain open. Under high shear in the microcirculation, VWF stretches out, exposing the cleavage site, and ADAMTS13 trims the ultra large multimers down to a manageable size. If ADAMTS13 is deficient or inhibited, as in TTP, those ultra large VWF multimers stay uncleaved and hyperreactive, recruiting excessive platelets and driving microvascular thrombosis. Know that ADAMTS13 itself has a modular structure too, metalloprotease, disintegrin, thrombospondin repeats, cysteine rich and spacer domains, and CUB domains, which mediate substrate recognition.
keypoints: ADAMTS13 cleaves VWF at Tyr1605-Met1606 within the A2 domain
Cleavage site is exposed only when shear force unfolds A2
A1 domain binds GPIb/collagen; A3 binds collagen
ADAMTS13 deficiency = uncleaved ultra-large VWF multimers -> platelet hyperaggregation
keypoint_voiceover: For boards, know that ADAMTS13 cleaves VWF specifically at tyrosine 1605 to methionine within the A2 domain, and this site is only exposed when shear force unfolds VWF in flowing blood. The A1 domain mediates platelet GPIb and collagen binding, while A3 binds collagen. When ADAMTS13 is deficient, ultra large VWF multimers go uncleaved, staying hyperadhesive and driving excessive platelet recruitment, which is the molecular basis of TTP.
